lines.text: The modern office has evolved dramatically, from traditional cubicle-based layouts to open-plan spaces, hot-desking environments, and hybrid home-office arrangements. A typical office contains workstations with desktop computers or laptops, monitors, keyboards, and mice. Desks may be height-adjustable (sit-stand desks) to promote better posture. The office kitchen or break room serves as a social hub where colleagues make tea, heat up lunch, and exchange small talk. Meeting rooms are equipped with projectors or screens, whiteboards, conference phones, and video conferencing systems. Filing cabinets, though increasingly rare in the digital age, still store physical documents. The reception area greets visitors with a front desk, seating area, and company branding. Office culture has its own language: 'hot-desking' means using any available desk rather than a fixed one; 'agile working' describes flexible arrangements; 'the water cooler' is a metaphor for informal conversation. Hierarchy is reflected in space — senior staff may have private offices, while junior employees share open areas. British offices emphasise tea rounds (taking turns to make tea for colleagues), cake on birthdays, and Friday afternoon informality. Understanding office vocabulary and culture is essential for anyone working in an English-speaking professional environment, from navigating the physical space to participating in the social rituals that build workplace relationships.

lines.text: In British offices, the 'tea round' is sacred. One person offers to make tea for the group ('Shall I put the kettle on?'), and everyone takes turns. Refusing to participate or always being 'too busy' when it's your turn is a genuine social faux pas.
